Glossary

indumentum
A covering of hairs or scales.
appressed
Lying flat against an object.
indumentum
A covering of hairs or scales.
key
(of fruit) Vernacular English term for winged samaras (as in e.g. Acer Fraxinus Ulmus)
midrib
midveinCentral and principal vein in a leaf.
monophyletic
(of a group of taxa) With a single ancestor; part of a natural lineage believed to reflect evolutionary relationships accurately (n. monophyly). (Cf. paraphyly polyphyly.)
taxon
(pl. taxa) Group of organisms sharing the same taxonomic rank (family genus species infraspecific variety).

Most garden stocks of Hydrangea villosa are probably descended from Ernest Wilson's 1908 introduction (Floors Castle, Scottish Borders; 13 August 2006). Image John Anderson.

Deciduous shrub, 1–3 m. Young branchlets angled, with white to yellow-brown hairs. Leaves opposite. Leaf blade elliptic to oblong-lanceolate, 10–20 × 3.5–6.5 cm; undersurface with spreading whitish hairs, with additional longer (to 3 mm) stiff, often brownish hairs on the midrib and larger veins; base acuminate; margin denticulate; apex acuminate; petiole 1–4 cm, with both hair types as on the veins. Inflorescence a terminal corymbose cyme, convex or flat; branches with white to brownish hairs; both fertile and sterile flowers present. Sterile flowers 3–4 cm across, largely consisting of ~4 petaloid sepals; sepals white to pink or lilac, orbicular-ovate, margins crenulate to entire. Fertile flowers with triangular calyx lobes barely half the length of the tube; petals ~5, free, purple to pink or blueish; stamens 10, unequal; ovary inferior; styles 2, spreading Fruit an urn-shaped capsule with truncate apex, 2.5–3 mm across, dehiscing apically, between the styles. Seeds brown, ~0.5 mm, winged at both ends. (Rehder in Sargent 1913; De Smet et al. 2017).

Distribution  China Hubei, Sichuan, perhaps more widely

Habitat Forest.

USDA Hardiness Zone 7-9

RHS Hardiness Rating H5

Conservation status Not evaluated (NE)

Belonging to the Hydrangea aspera complex, the status of H. villosa is still contested (see H. aspera for general discussion of the group). To gardeners though, the name usefully singles out a group of plants (mostly descended from a single wild collection over 100 years ago) with smaller, narrower leaves and smaller inflorescences than many other asperas, a usefully dense, compact habit, as well as a distinctive type of dense indumentum on the leaf undersides. This taxon includes some of the finest plants in the complex for general garden use.

The hairs on the leaf underside have always been key to defining H. villosa (Sargent 1913; De Smet et al. 2017). Firstly, short, stiff, spreading white hairs thickly cover every vein, down to the very smallest, so one can hardly tell that they are restricted to the veins. On the midrib and secondary veins these are joined by longer hairs, to about 3 mm long, which are variably yellowish to brownish (as ever with hydrangeas, ‘-ish’ needs emphasizing); the overall effect is a coarsely velvety feel. H. strigosa has only the shorter white hairs, and these are both stiffer and appressed, a very different look under a lens. Both these Chinese species were first described by Rehder (in Sargent 1913) from Ernest Wilson’s W Sichuan specimens, H. villosa from W 1227 & 1250 of 1908 and W 4302 & 4483 of 1910. McClintock (1957) sank H. villosa into H. aspera subsp. aspera, a view shared (a little surprisingly) by both authors of the Flora of China account (Wei & Bartholomew 2001); Chinese botanists still tend not to recognize the species (Chinese Academy of Sciences 2024). The need for a name to cover what is – at least in gardens – a reasonably distinct swarm of cultivars and unnamed seedlings resulted in H. aspera Villosa Group being coined, a tag commonly seen today (e.g. Edwards & Marshall 2019; Dirr 2021). However, the concept of H. villosa is far from dead to science. A cytological study using numbers of living plants in the French reference collection at Angers divided H. aspera subsp. aspera into Kawakamii (Taiwanese) and Villosa groups, based on differences in chromosomal organization (Mortreau et al. 2010). These authors suggested reinstating both of these as species, although the implication is that no plants in the study would then represent H. aspera s.s. (whatever that might be). The DNA-based study of De Smet et al. (2017) who had found plants matching the Sichuan type of H. villosa during fieldwork in Hubei, gave rather good support to H. villosa as a distinct, monophyletic grouping. These authors too recommended accepting H. villosa and H. kawakamii, but this time as distinct from a narrow-sense H. aspera.

H. villosa was introduced to Western gardens from Wilson’s 1908 collections (Haworth-Booth 1984) although it seems impossible today to find clonal material under a Wilson number. Cuttings are not always easy to root (Haworth-Booth 1984) and generations of seed-raising have resulted in a rather variable garden population, probably due to both reassortment of genes from the original plants and outcrossing to other asperas. Indumentum aside, what they have in common is smaller, narrower leaves than many others in the H. aspera complex; flowers July–August (S England) in smaller inflorescences than many, with usually pinkish or lilac sterile flowers and variably purple fertile flowers; and a relatively compact, dense habit which suits them to mixed borders (Foster 2023). Partial shade in soil which does not get too dry is ideal. Several of the best cultivars belong in – or at least have a lot to do with – H. villosa, including ‘Anthony Bullivant’, ‘Sam MacDonald’ and ‘Velvet and Lace’ (listed with all others in the complex under Hydrangea aspera Species Complex Cultivars).

A few newer introductions have probably contributed little to the garden gene pool as yet. These include WD 042 (a NACPEC collection from Hubei, 1994) as grown at the Arnold Arboretum, MA, the Morris Arboretum, PA and San Francisco Botanical Garden (Arnold Arboretum 2024; Quarryhill Botanical Garden 2024), and SICH 900 (Sichuan 1994) as grown at Sonoma Botanical Garden, CA (Quarryhill Botanical Garden 2024). DJHG 11061 (Guizhou 2011) has been attributed to this species; making ‘magnificent’ 3.7 m tall shrubs at Windcliff, Washington State, it has been offered commercially in a small way: ‘finest for the PNW’ (Pacific Northwest) enthuses Dan Hinkley (2024).

Summer flowering Hydrangea villosa, with every inflorescence at the same stage, giving floral impact rather than staying power (Plas Newydd, Anglesey, UK; 3 August 2018). Image John Anderson.

Hydrangea villosa, as seen in gardens, makes a usefully compact, rather dense summer-flowering shrub (Cholmondeley Castle, Cheshire, UK; 26 July 2024). Image Barry Grain.

Hydrangea villosa includes some of the finest members of the H. aspera complex for general garden use (Cholmondeley Castle, Cheshire, UK; 26 July 2024). Image Barry Grain.

The pale, peeling bark of Hydrangea villosa (in the cultivar 'Velvet and Lace', White House Farm, Kent, UK; 12 July 2023). Image Julian Sutton.

Relatively small leaves, dense hairs and compact habit give Hydrangea villosa much of its character in the garden (private garden, Ayrshire, UK; 14 August 2023). Image Julian Sutton.

Hydrangea villosa has two types of hair on the leaf undersurface, stiff, spreading, white ones densely covering all veins down to the very smallest, with longer, often yellow or brownish ones scattered amongst them on the midrib and secondary veins (White House Farm, Kent, UK; 12 July 2023). Image Julian Sutton.

Hydrangea villosa has smaller, narrower leaves than most others in the H. aspera complex (White House Farm, Kent, UK; 12 July 2023). Image Julian Sutton.
